senses.def: the handmaid of Sarah and the concubine of Abraham and mother of Ishmael (Galatians 4:24)

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: an activity which is unjust
reason or cause for an event or state
(a technical, legal term) the basis of or grounds for an accusation in court
senses.comment: In rendering αἰτία[b] as basis for an accusation, one may sometimes speak of a reason for accusing someone or why someone should be accused of something bad.|For another interpretation of αἰτία in John 18:38, see 88.315.

senses.def: the content of legal charges brought against someone

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: guilt as a basis or reason for condemnation
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand αἰτία in John 18:38 as ‘reason for legal accusation,’ as noted in 56.4.

senses.def: a relation existing between two or more objects or events
the content of that which is true and thus in accordance with what actually happened
senses.comment: In John 8:32 ἀλήθεια is used to refer to the revelation of God that Jesus brings or, perhaps, to Jesus himself for what he actually is as the revelation of God.

senses.def: (idioms, literally: ‘in truth,’ ‘upon truth,’ and ‘according to truth’) pertaining to being a real or actual event or state
young of sheep πρόβατον; often used for ritual sacrifice
senses.comment: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between male and female lambs. It is therefore essential in any figurative reference to male persons to employ an appropriate term for lamb. In a number of languages, of course, a lamb is simply referred to as a ‘young sheep’ or ‘child sheep.’|Perhaps the most widespread story about cultural differences in Bible translation is the one which refers to the translation of ‘lamb’ as ‘little seal of God’ in an Eskimo language. However, there is no evidence that this type of rendering was ever used, since in matters of appearance, habitat, and behavior, lambs and little seals have practically nothing in common. Furthermore, Eskimo languages have terms for ‘lamb’ and in some instances, at least, use the expression ‘young, woolly goat,’ since wild goats are well known and wool is well known as an imported product.

senses.def: to bring everything together in terms of some unifying principle or person
pertaining to one who cannot be accused of anything wrong
senses.comment: In a number of languages the phrase ‘without accusations’ must be rendered by a clause, for example, ‘in such a way that no one can accuse you of doing wrong’ or ‘without the possibility of anyone accusing you.’

senses.def: one who brings an accusation against someone
one who is actively and continuously hostile toward someone
a person for whom there is no record of a male parent or who has never had a male parent or whose father has died
to close off an area, and in the process of doing so, to exclude
to lose one’s consciousness temporarily
senses.comment: It is possible that ἀποψύχω in Luke 21:26 refers primarily to a psychological experience rather than a physiological one. Some scholars, however, have interpreted ἀποψύχω in this context as meaning ‘to die.’ For another interpretation of ἀποψύχω in Luke 21:26, see ἀποψύχω[b] 25.293.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἀποψύχω[a] ‘to faint,’ 23.184) to become totally disheartened and thus ready to give up
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀποψύχω in Luke 21:26, see ἀποψύχω[a] 23.184.

senses.def: a cloth attached above a boat in such a way as to catch the wind and thus propel the boat through the water
senses.comment: In Acts 27:40 (the only occurrence of ἀρτέμων in the NT) the reference may be to the foresail, that is, a relatively small sail toward the prow of the ship. A sail may be described in some languages as ‘a piece of cloth to make the ship move’ or ‘cloth on the ship to catch the wind.’

senses.def: a person greeted in the Epistle to the Romans

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: the quality of integrity as an expression of moral soundness
pertaining to being relatively heavy
senses.comment: Although the meaning of βαρύς in Matthew 23:4 is literal, the entire expression is figurative, and so it may be necessary in some languages to say ‘they fix up heavy loads, so to speak, and tie them on people’s backs.’

senses.def: pertaining to that which is difficult in view of its being burdensome
senses.comment: In rendering ‘his commandments are not burdensome,’ it may be necessary in some languages to translate ‘it is not difficult to do what he has commanded.’

senses.def: pertaining to being important in view of substantive character
pertaining to one who is vicious and cruel
senses.comment: In a number of languages a strictly literal translation of Acts 20:29 might be misunderstood. It may therefore be important to translate the last part of this expression as ‘people like cruel wolves will come among you.’

senses.def: to conduct oneself, with focus upon everyday activity
a disease involving severe inflammation and possibly a cancerous spread of ulcers which eat away the flesh and bones
pertaining to possessing purported good character or quality
to cause someone to suffer public disgrace or shame
senses.comment: The expression ‘to disgrace in public’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘to cause everyone to think bad about’ or ‘to cause everyone to speak in whispers about.’

senses.def: to provide specific information (especially with regard to some future contingency)
to announce extensively and publicly
a clear or marked distinction

senses.subdomain: Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
senses.def: a stone which has fallen from heaven or the sky (originally employed in referring to images of the gods)
senses.comment: The object referred to by τοῦ διοπετοῦς in Acts 19:35 was probably a stone meteorite regarded as a sacred supernatural object.

senses.def: to move or sink down, especially of the sun sinking below the horizon
the surface of the earth
to be absent from a place where one rightfully or normally belongs
(an idiom, literally: to leave home from the body) euphemistic expressions for dying
to cause an object to extend in space (for example, by becoming straight, unfolded, or uncoiled)
(an idiom, literally to stretch out hands upon) to take a person into custody for alleged illegal activity
to keep a record of something
senses.comment: There may be difficulties involved in changing the passive expression ‘no account is kept of sins’ in Romans 5:13 to ‘God doesn’t keep an account of sins,’ for this might imply that God was unconcerned about sin. It is sometimes possible to avoid this difficulty by rendering ‘no account is kept of sins’ as ‘a sin is not listed as a sin.’

senses.def: to charge to an account

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: any kind of clothing

(figurative extension of meaning of ἐξαγοράζω ‘to pay a price,’ not occurring in the NT) to cause the release or freedom of someone by a means which proves costly to the individual causing the release
senses.comment: A literal rendering of ἀγοράζω[b] or ἐξαγοράζω as ‘to release by means of paying a price’ can be misinterpreted in the sense that Christ actually engaged in some kind of monetary transaction. A literal translation may also lead to the mistaken interpretation, which was widespread in the Middle Ages, that in redeeming the believers God actually paid a price to the Devil. Obviously, ἀγοράζω in 1 Corinthians 6:20 and ἐξαγοράζω in Galatians 3:13 must be understood in a figurative sense.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to buy out the time) to take full advantage of any opportunity
glosses: to make good use of every opportunity
to take advantage of every chance
senses.comment: The implication of this statement in Colossians 4:5 is taking advantage of every opportunity to manifest the reality of one’s faith.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to redeem the time) to do something with intensity and urgency (used absolutely)
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret ἐξαγοράζομαι τὸν καιρόν in Ephesians 5:16 as ‘to take full advantage of every opportunity’ (see 65.42).

senses.def: to speak of the excellence of a person, object, or event
senses.comment: In a number of languages praise can only be expressed by direct discourse, and this requires some content which provides the basis for praise. For example, in Luke 2:13 instead of a literal rendering of ‘praising God,’ it may be necessary to have ‘they said, God is wonderful,’ and in Luke 16:8 it may be necessary to translate ‘the master of this dishonest manager said, You are remarkable for having done such a clever thing.’

senses.def: that which is worthy of or deserves praise
senses.comment: In some languages the closest equivalent of ‘praiseworthy’ is ‘something which people should praise.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: the quality of gracious forbearing

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Marking and Writing
senses.def: an object containing writing addressed to one or more persons
senses.comment: In some languages it may be necessary to try to distinguish between a letter as an object and a letter as content or message. In Acts 23:33 the focus seems to be upon the letter as an object, not necessarily upon the contents of the document. In most contexts, however, it is impossible to distinguish between a letter as a material object and a letter as a message (see 33.48).

senses.def: a written communication, usually from one person to one or more persons
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand ἐπιστολή in Acts 23:25 not as a content or message, but as an object (see 6.63)

senses.def: a Greek god
a person greeted in Romans 16:14
(derivative of εὐλογέω[a] ‘to praise,’ 33.356) pertaining to being worthy of praise or commendation
kind of poisonous snake; associated with lurking danger
senses.comment: The terms ἀσπίς and ἔχιδνα[a] may be used to refer to almost any kind of poisonous snake, and since at least some type of poisonous snake occurs in practically all parts of the world, there is usually little difficulty involved in finding an appropriate term. One can, however, always employ a descriptive expression, for example, ‘a snake whose bite causes death.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἔχιδνα[a] ‘viper,’ 4.53) a dangerous and despised person
senses.comment: One must exercise due caution in rendering ἔχιδνα in Matthew 12:34 and ὄφις[b] in Matthew 23:33, since in some cultures snakes are regarded as being particularly wise and clever, and therefore an expression such as ‘brood of vipers’ could be a compliment. In some languages important distinctions are made between different types of snakes, and therefore connotations may vary considerably.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to a quiet, peaceful existence or attitude
(derivative of θερίζω ‘to harvest,’ 43.14) a person who gathers in a crop
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no specific term for ‘reapers,’ and therefore it may be necessary in Matthew 13:30 to say ‘… I will say to those who are working in the fields’ or ‘… who are cutting down the grain.’

senses.def: an Egyptian sorcerer who together with Jambres opposed Moses before Pharaoh
the state of being asleep
senses.comment: In some languages sleep is expressed by an idiom, for example, ‘his soul had wandered away’ or ‘his eyes had disappeared.’ Though an expression such as ‘his soul had wandered away’ might appear in some languages to have misleading theological implications, it really means only ‘to sleep.’

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of καθεύδω[a] ‘to sleep,’ 23.66) to sleep, as a euphemistic expression for the state of being dead
senses.comment: Some translators have attempted to preserve the figure of speech in καθεύδω[b] and κοιμάομαι[b] by translating to sleep rather than to have died or to be dead. Such a practice, however, has resulted in misunderstanding in a number of instances and has sometimes led to the doctrine of so-called soul-sleep.

senses.def: a rule involving a standard for conduct
an area of activity, defined geographically and functionally
to leave or depart, with emphasis on the finality of the action
to cause or permit something to remain in a place and to go away (with or without implying purpose)
to cause to continue to exist, normally referring to a small part of a larger whole

senses.subdomain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
senses.def: to give up or neglect one’s concern for something
glosses: to no longer be concerned about
to give up one’s concern for

senses.def: to cause a particular relationship to cease
senses.comment: In rendering Ephesians 5:31 it is important to avoid an expression which will suggest abandoning or deserting. It is the limitation of a particular relationship which is involved.

senses.def: to leave someone without help (possibly in the sense of ‘to cease helping’)
to cause to pour down on

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the hard bony outgrowth on the heads of certain animals
senses.comment: Finding a term for ‘horn’ is usually not at all difficult. The problem arises when a term for ‘horn’ is already employed in a receptor language as a euphemistic expression for the male genital organ. It may therefore be necessary in Revelation 5:6 to speak of ‘a lamb with seven horns on his head.’|In speaking of the horn-shaped corners of the altar (Revelation 9:13), it is often better not to use a term meaning literally horn, since this might imply that the altar had the horns of animals stuck on to the corners. One can normally say ‘corners of the altar shaped like horns’ or ‘… looking like horns or projections on the corners of the altar.’ See 79.105.

senses.def: a projection at the corner of an object
(a figurative extension of meaning of κέρας[a] ‘horn,’ 8.17) power of unusual significance
senses.comment: In Luke 1:69 the reference of the phrase κέρας σωτηρίας is to the role of the Messiah, and accordingly one may often best render this phrase as ‘mighty Savior’ or ‘powerful Savior.’

senses.def: to take secretly and without permission the property of someone else
a group of soldiers serving as a guard

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to bend over into a stooping position
a city in Lycaonia in Asia Minor

senses.subdomain: Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
senses.def: a colorful, relatively hard form of limestone which may be polished to a lustrous finish (especially valued as material for building or for sculpture)
senses.comment: Where there is no technical term for ‘marble,’ one may use an expression such as ‘beautiful rock’ or ‘valuable stone.’

senses.def: (derivative of μερίζω[a] ‘to divide,’ 63.23) one who divides

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
senses.def: an indefinite negated point of time
pertaining to not being certain
marker of negative purpose, often with the implication of apprehension
to learn the secret of something through personal experience or as the result of initiation
a person greeted in Romans 16:15
pertaining to not being previously known and hence unheard of and unfamiliar

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a person belonging to a socio-political group other than the reference group
senses.comment: Terms for ‘stranger’ or ‘foreigner’ are often based upon geographical differences or upon lack of previous knowledge. For example, ‘I was a stranger’ may be rendered as ‘I came from another country’ or ‘I was not known to any of you.’

senses.def: a person who shows hospitality to guests
senses.comment: In rendering ‘host’ it may be necessary to employ a phrase, for example, ‘who welcomed and took care of us in his home.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to regard something or someone as of little value
(derivative of ὁράω[a] ‘to see,’ 24.1) that which is seen
an event in which something appears vividly and credibly to the mind, although not actually present, but implying the influence of some divine or supernatural power or agency
the sky as a source or as a location from which implied movement takes place
senses.comment: οὐρανόθεν in Acts 14:17 and Acts 26:13 is somewhat ambiguous, for both events may be regarded as involving a semantic derivative of οὐρανός[b] heaven (1.11) rather than οὐρανός[a] sky (1.5). In Acts 14:17 one might very well translate ‘he gives rain from heaven,’ since obviously the agent is God. Similarly, in Acts 26:13 the light might come from heaven, since the light is presumably regarded as a supernatural phenomenon.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: unlimited duration of time, with particular focus upon the future
senses.comment: For another interpretation of εἰς τὸ παντελές in Hebrews 7:25, see 78.47.

senses.def: a degree of completeness, with the possible implication of purpose or result
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand the phrase εἰς τὸ παντελές as meaning ‘forever’ (see 67.95).|It is possible to translate this expression in Luke 13:11 as ‘she could not straighten up at all.’ The difference of interpretation in Luke 13:11 depends upon the scope of the phrase εἰς τὸ παντελές. If this phrase qualifies the negation, then the rendering is ‘she could not straighten up at all,’ but if the phrase εἰς τὸ παντελές qualifies just ἀνακύψαι, then the appropriate meaning would be ‘she could not straighten up completely.’

senses.subdomain: Units of Time with Reference to Other Units or Points of Time: Yesterday, Today, Next Day
senses.def: a day on which preparations were made for a sacred or feast day
senses.comment: The identification of παρασκευή with Friday became so traditional that it eventually came to be the present-day Greek term for ‘Friday.’

senses.def: (derivative of πατήρ[c] ‘ancestor, forefather,’ 10.20) pertaining to one’s ancestors
to cover by putting something around
a procurator of Judea who gave the order for the crucifixion of Jesus
air in relatively rapid movement, but without specification as to the force of the movement
senses.comment: As in the case of English (which has, for example, such terms as breeze, zephyr, gust, storm, whirlwind, cyclone, tornado, etc.), other languages likewise normally have a number of different terms depending upon the strength of the wind and whether the wind may be carrying substances such as sand or dust. In some languages there may also be a problem involved in the use of terms for ‘wind,’ since some of these may have meanings of malicious or malevolent spirits, or they may imply a disease-bringing event.

senses.def: the process of breathing
senses.comment: Rather than rendering Acts 17:25 as ‘gives life and breath to all people,’ it may be better to say ‘causes all people to live and breathe.’ In some languages, however, ‘to breathe’ is synonymous with ‘life,’ and therefore to say ‘to live and to breathe’ is to be both redundant and repetitious. One may therefore translate ‘who causes all people to live.’

senses.def: to cause to drink
senses.comment: In some languages it is impossible to avoid a reference to what is drunk. Therefore, one may translate Matthew 25:35 as ‘I was thirsty and you gave me water to drink.’

senses.def: to provide water for plants
senses.comment: In a number of languages one not speak of ‘watering a plant,’ but one may ‘water the ground’ or ‘cause the ground to drink’ or ‘make the ground muddy.’

senses.def: a rain occurring early in the autumn, September or October, in contrast with normal rains occurring in the middle of the winter season
senses.comment: See 14.13.|In Palestine the rainy season differs appreciably from what it is in many other parts of the world. In tropical regions north of the Equator, the rains occur primarily from May through October, and in the tropical regions below the Equator, the rains normally occur from November through April. The other seasons of the year are normally quite dry. In Palestine, however, rains occur primarily during the months of November through March, and the summer months are often without rain. Because of this significant difference in the time of rainfall, it may be important to relate the early and late rains not to particular times of the year but to the normal period for rain. For example, the early rains could be ‘rain coming before it is normally expected’ or ‘rain at the beginning of the rainy season,’ and late rains are ‘rains which come later than what one expects’ or ‘rain at the end of the rainy season.’ On the other hand, the contrast may be expressed as ‘rain coming before it should’ or ‘rain coming later than it should.’ It is difficult to relate early and late rains to so-called ‘growing seasons,’ since in the Middle East grains grow primarily during the rainy season and are harvested early in the spring, while fruits and vegetables are grown in the spring and summer with extensive use made of irrigation.

senses.def: that which causes someone to stumble
an occasion or reason for taking offense
glosses: what causes someone to be offended

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: that which provides an opportunity or occasion for causing someone to sin
glosses: that which causes someone to sin or that which provides an occasion for someone to sin

senses.def: rights associated with being the firstborn
to hit or strike with the open hand, the fist, or an instrument (for example, club, rod, or whip)
(derivative of Σαμάρεια ‘Samaria,’ 93.568) a person who is a native of Samaria
an intoxicating drink made from grain
senses.comment: Though σίκερα may have a generic meaning and thus refer to any type of intoxicating drink, in the NT it occurs only in Luke 1:15, where it contrasts with wine and refers to intoxicating beverages made from grain. Distilled alcoholic beverages, such as whiskey, gin, and vodka, were not known in the ancient world.

senses.def: a city on the west coast of Asia Minor
a wreath consisting either of foliage or of precious metals formed to resemble foliage and worn as a symbol of honor, victory, or as a badge of high office
senses.comment: It may be important in some contexts to indicate clearly the significance of the wreath worn on the head, for example, ‘a wreath to show victory.’ To describe ‘a wreath’ merely as ‘a circle of leaves’ would hardly be sufficient to indicate its cultural significance. In order to do justice to the cultural relevance of such a wreath, it may be important to add some type of marginal note (compare διάδημα ‘diadem crown,’ 6.196).

senses.def: a prize or reward given as the result of outstanding performance
senses.comment: In Revelation 2:10 the relationship between τὸν στέφανον and τῆς ζωῆς is one of apposition, for the prize consists of life. Essentially the same relationship exists in the construction ἀπόκειταί μοι ὁ τῆς δικαιοσύνης στέφανος ‘the prize of righteousness awaits me’ 2 Timothy 4:8. In this case the prize is ‘being declared righteous’ or ‘being put right with God.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of στέφανος[a] ‘wreath, crown,’ 6.192) a symbol of successful activity
to enjoy a state of happiness or well-being together with someone else
coming to an agreement with, often implying a type of joint decision
to conduct oneself in relation to a person with whom one lives
a leader of a synagogue in Corinth
senses.comment: Many scholars consider Σωσθένης[a] and Σωσθένης[b] to be the same person.

senses.def: a Christian of Corinth
senses.comment: Many scholars consider Σωσθένης[a] and Σωσθένης[b] to be the same person.

senses.def: (derivative of τελέω[e] ‘to pay taxes,’ 57.178) one who collects taxes for the government
senses.comment: Since Jews who farmed the taxes for the Romans (that is to say, who paid Roman authorities for the privilege of collecting taxes) were considered traitors to their own people, the term τελώνης has strongly negative connotations in the NT. In any translation of the Gospels it may be especially important to have an adequate marginal note designed to explain the basis for the hostility which many people had toward tax collectors.

senses.def: a generic expression for any type of table
(a figurative extension of meaning of τράπεζα[a] ‘table,’ 6.113) a meal, with possible emphasis upon its being relatively bountiful
a place where money is kept or managed or where credit is established

senses.subdomain: Belong To, Be Included in the Membership of, Be Excluded From
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to share in a table) to belong to a particular religious group as evidenced by ceremonial eating
glosses: to eat at the table of

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to serve tables) to be responsible for financial aspects of an enterprise
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret the phrase διακονέω τραπέζαις not as an idiom but simply as ‘to wait on tables, to serve meals’ (see 23.26 and 46.13), but even so the context relates to caring for needs.

senses.def: (derivative of ὕαλος[a] ‘glass,’ 6.222) consisting of or pertaining to glass
a position below another position or object
(with the accusative) a marker of a controlling person, institution, or power
senses.comment: It is generally a mistake to render literally the expression τοὺς ὑπὸ νόμον as in Galatians 4:5, because ‘those who are under the Law’ may simply mean ‘people who act illegally.’

senses.subdomain: Agent, Personal or Nonpersonal, Causative or Immediate, Direct or Indirect
senses.def: (with the genitive) a marker of agent or force, whether person or event
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is difficult, if not impossible, to use a so-called passive expression which introduces an agent by means of a preposition. It may, therefore, be necessary in a number of instances to make the agent the subject of the sentence or clause. For example, Mark 1:13 may be restructured as ‘Satan tempted Jesus when Jesus was in the desert for forty days.’

senses.def: a marker of cause or reason, with focus upon instrumentality, either of objects or events

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: a marker of the approximate time of a period (a rare usage)
(an idiom, literally: to fall under judgment) to be condemned for acting contrary to laws and regulations
senses.comment: In the context of James 5:12 the condemnation refers to God’s judgment.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: under the sky) pertaining to being on the earth
senses.comment: ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανόν is essentially equivalent in reference to ἐπίγειος ‘on the earth’ (1.41).

senses.def: to be under the complete control of someone
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is simply not possible to preserve the idiom ‘under the feet of,’ though in some instances one may use a parallel idiom, for example, ‘to stand on,’ so that 1 Corinthians 15:25 might be rendered ‘until he stands on all his enemies,’ but it is more likely that the idiom in this context is better rendered as ‘until he defeats all his enemies.’

senses.def: to cause something to be fully known by revealing clearly and in some detail
a person of professional or semi-professional status regarded as having particular capacity or competence in understanding the meaning or significance of human experience
senses.comment: In some instances φιλόσοφος in Acts 17:18 may be translated simply as ‘teacher,’ since such a word would normally designate a professional or semi-professional person involved in scholarly activities.

senses.def: to grow (of plants)
senses.comment: In Hebrews 12:15 φύω occurs in an extended figurative context which may be better treated as a simile. Compare, for example, a literal translation of μή τις ῥίζα πικρίας ἄνω φύουσα ‘lest any root of bitterness grow up’ with the treatment of this expression as a type of simile, ‘in order that no one becomes like a bitter plant that grows up.’

senses.def: hairy four-legged mammal with hoofs, brown or gray in color; non-ruminant and omnivorous; Sus scrofa; domesticated land animal; unclean, not to be eaten; regarded as an ugly, filthy, and destructive animal and often associated with pagan rituals
senses.comment: Though references to pigs in the OT frequently involve very strong connotations of uncleanness and disgust, references in the NT are somewhat more neutral. However, in the story of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:15) the reference to the task of feeding swine certainly indicates the desperate condition of the younger brother. Some translators have found it necessary to indicate such a fact by a marginal note, since the language into which the translation is being made may reflect a very different cultural attitude from that which occurs in the Scriptures. For example, in certain areas of New Guinea, one who is responsible for taking care of pigs is an individual with relatively high social status.

senses.def: to touch by feeling and handling, implying movement over a surface
senses.comment: There are a number of problems involved in the rendering of 1 John 1:1, for there are several radical shifts in figurative meaning. The specific reference is to ‘the Word of life’ which seems like a purposely ambiguous reference to Jesus Christ. The statement about ‘hearing the Word’ would seem to refer to a message, but the reference to ‘seeing’ implies some type of object. To emphasize the concrete nature of such an object (namely, the person of Christ), this statement about ‘touching’ is included, but in some languages a reference to ‘feeling and handling’ might imply quite a wrong connotation or even improper activity, particularly if the object involved is specifically a person.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ψηλαφάω[a] ‘to touch, to feel,’ 24.76) to make an effort, despite difficulties, to come to know something, when the chances of success in such an enterprise are not particularly great
